newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin comes through seven-hour heart operation.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin comes through seven-hour heart operation.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin came through seven hours of open heart surgery on Tuesday, although it may be several days before doctors can be certain that the 65-year-old Russian president will make a complete recovery.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Russian news agencies that the multiple bypass operation, which Yeltsin hopes can give him strength to end months of political in-fighting, "ended successfully at 2 p.m.".
A source at Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre told Reuters: "Everything was fine, great...He is OK."
The president will take some hours to shrug off the effects of the anaesthetic and it may be some time after that before he feels well enough to take back power from his prime minister.

Yeltsin, said to be cracking jokes before going under the anaesthetic, temporarily handed over power, including the nuclear trigger, to Viktor Chernomyrdin, one of several figures jostling for position around the sick president.
Yeltsin issued a written statement saying he was confident of recovery and reassuring Russians there was no power vacuum.
"Not for a minute will the country be without a leader with full powers," Yeltsin said. "He (Chernomyrdin) and my other colleagues are tested and reliable people."
Chernomyrdin, 58, and a possible successor, has effectively been running the country since Yeltsin's reelection on July 3.

As Yeltsin went under the surgeon's knife, tens of thousands marched in Russia's Far East in strikes and demonstrations called by trade unions to protest over unpaid wages -- the most potent symbol of the country's massive economic problems.

Chernomyrdin ordered payments to several sectors, including education and health, to be speeded up and increased. But that will not help millions of military personnel and private sector workers who are owed the bulk of some $8 billion in back-pay.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who faces reelection on Tuesday, sent Yeltsin "best wishes for a speedy recovery". The Russian Orthodox Church has called for prayers.
Western leaders see Yeltsin, who led Russia out of communism in 1991, as the best guarantor of Russia's shaky democracy and fear his loss could plunge it into a period of deep instability.
Bypass surgery improves blood supply to the heart by grafting in veins to divert blood around blockages -- in Yeltsin's case three or four -- in the cardiac arteries.
It was performed by Renat Akchurin, 50, who previously also gave Chernomyrdin a bypass. He worked with a team of three other Russian surgeons and eight assistants.
Michael DeBakey, the 88-year-old U.S. cardiologist who pioneered the bypass technique more than 30 years ago, monitored the operation nearby.
Hundreds of bypass operations are performed around the world every day. Only some two percent fail.
Medical experts say the biggest risk to the president may be problems with other organs, like his liver. Two German doctors specialised in post-operative complications are on hand.
The president had announced the operation on television in a moment of unprecedented candour on September 5.
That ended weeks of equivocation by aides who had been explaining Yeltsin's absence since before his reelection by saying he had a cold and various other minor ailments.
The admission that the president, who had two heart attacks last year, needed major surgery also fueled a bitter struggle for influence in the Kremlin.
It involved notably Chernomyrdin, chief of the presidential staff Anatoly Chubais and General Alexander Lebed, a political maverick roped in to the Kremlin to secure victory at the polls.

Yeltsin finally sacked Lebed on October 17 amid a flurry of accusations and counter-accusations of mysterious plots and plans to seize power. Lebed has warned of an army mutiny over unpaid wages, but few analysts see a military bid for power.

The 46-year-old former paratrooper, his popularity assured by his success in ending the deeply unpopular Chechen war, remains a key political figure. Polls show he would be a strong contender for the presidency if Yeltsin had to step down.
If that were to happen Chernomyrdin would rule in the interim with a mandate to hold an election within three months.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, would also be a challenger in a new vote. He complained the Kremlin cheated to beat him in July by concealing that Yeltsin had had a third heart attack days before the second-round vote.
